paras: The killing of Sarah Nealy was the death of a Black woman held as a laborer on Fletcher Turner's plantation about seven miles west of Dadeville, in Tallapoosa County, Alabama, after she was whipped, hung by the wrists and struck with a pistol, according to an affidavit of six Black witnesses.
The account surfaced in June 1903 during a federal peonage inquiry and was printed across the country, while Turner said the woman died of disease.

In 1903 a federal grand jury at Montgomery heard evidence that Tallapoosa and Coosa planters held Black laborers in servitude by paying their fines on petty charges and working them under guard. Fletcher (J. F.) Turner leased county convicts, and his son Allen, about 17, was arrested in June on three peonage indictments naming other laborers.

According to the affidavit, the woman came to Turner's place on a Monday and was set to piling brush in "the new ground." When she could not work as wanted, Allen Turner whipped her with a buggy trace, 100 lashes, while two laborers held her, then had her handcuffed and drawn up by the wrists over a tree limb for about two hours. Let down at dinner, she crawled into some bushes, refused bread and later said she could not see; she lay down behind a brush pile, and the witnesses said Turner "beat her over the head with a pistol again and she died."

A second version, from a New York Evening Post correspondent, named no one and said a "guard" struck her with his pistol and "jumped upon her stomach"; she was found dead about three o'clock. Grand jury witnesses said she was buried at night in a rough box with two people present, while the Montgomery dispatch placed the burial the next morning at Eagle church.

The Tallapoosa County grand jury, then sitting at Dadeville, took up the death. According to the Chicago Chronicle correspondent, the Turners shackled the witnesses together and warned them they would not live to reach court unless they called it a natural death; they complied, and the case was dismissed.

In federal court the Turners faced peonage charges, not murder, and the Cleveland Gazette noted that none of the accused would be punished for the killing itself. When the Turners appeared for trial on July 6, the Montgomery Advertiser reported that the district attorney was expected to nolle prosse the cases alleging they beat to death "a negro girl, Sarah Healy." Two days later it reported that Allen Turner's cases had been continued and that a case over Cornelia Hammock, a county convict at Turner's place, had not been pressed. The Indianapolis Freeman wrote that Turner and his guards Allen Turner and Robert Barron were to be sentenced, but no report of a conviction for the woman's death was found.

Northern white papers first carried the affidavit in a St. Louis Republic feature of June 21, "Twenty-Two Indicted for Torturing Negroes," which called her fate "a typical example" of peonage. A syndicated item, "Slavery in Alabama," told of "the murder of Sarah Nealy" in Wisconsin and Ohio weeklies, and the Evening Post version ran under headlines such as "The Horrors of Peonage" in the Minneapolis Journal.

Alabama papers took another line: the Montgomery Advertiser printed Turner's denial of the claims of "sensational newspapers," and the Birmingham Age-Herald declared there was "not a bit of truth" in the stories.

The Black press relied on the Chronicle account: the Iowa Bystander reprinted a Register and Leader editorial likening the tortures to Kishinev. The Cleveland Gazette ran it on its July 4 front page as "Poor Sarah Nealy's Fate" and closed with the gibe that "Great" is Alabama justice and law, and the Freeman cited it among the worst peonage cases.

The six witnesses described a beating death, while Fletcher Turner said the woman died of disease; his denial names her Cornelia Hammock, and the papers do not say whether she and Sarah Nealy were the same person. Accounts also differ on who struck her: the affidavit names Allen Turner, the Evening Post version an unnamed guard, and the Freeman Turner and two guards.

reader.title: Killing of Sarah Nealy
bases: She was a laborer held on Fletcher Turner's convict-leasing plantation and was beaten to death for not working as wanted (A5, A14, A17).

She was killed illegally per the witnesses (A3, A5), but by an employer's son, alone or with one or two guards (A6, A21), as labor discipline, not by a group acting under a pretext of justice or tradition.
The affidavit (A2, A5, A13) and an independent Evening Post account (A7, A20) agree on a beating death, but Fletcher Turner denies it (A17) and the Age-Herald calls the stories untrue (A22).

accounts.label: Witnesses' affidavit (Chicago Chronicle correspondent)
accounts.gist: Six Black laborers swore Allen Turner whipped her 100 lashes, hung her by handcuffed wrists from a tree limb two hours, and beat her with a pistol until she died.

accounts.label: New York Evening Post correspondent / Montgomery dispatch
accounts.gist: An unnamed guard beat, hung and struck the woman with a pistol and jumped on her stomach; she died about 3; witnesses were marched under guard to the grand jury and kept silent from fear.

accounts.label: Fletcher Turner (defendant)
accounts.gist: Turner said the woman, Cornelia Hammock, was not beaten to death by his son but died of disease and was buried respectably.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Freeman
accounts.gist: B. F. Turner and guards Allen Turner and Robert Barron beat a negress and strung her up by the wrists; she died the day after she was turned over to Turner on a trumped-up charge.

framing.detail: St. Louis Republic headline 'Twenty-Two Indicted for Torturing Negroes' and 'Negroes Whipped to Death'; calls her fate typical of peonage.
Syndicated 'Slavery in Alabama' calls it 'the murder of Sarah Nealy' in Wisconsin and Ohio weeklies.
Bottineau Courant editorial: 'inhuman monsters who beat a poor negress to death escaped punishment'.
Minneapolis Journal 'The Horrors of Peonage'; Black Hills Union 'Pass Cruelties of Ante Bellum Days' (unnamed victim).
Montgomery Advertiser reports court steps and gives Fletcher Turner's denial against 'sensational newspapers'.
Birmingham Age-Herald editorial: 'not a bit of truth' in the stories; 'a fig-nt of some disordered brain'; attacks the Evening Post as sectional.
Iowa Bystander reprints editorial likening the tortures to Kishinev and recalling Uncle Tom's Cabin.
Cleveland Gazette front page 'Simply Barbarous' / 'Poor Sarah Nealy's Fate', ending '"Great" is Alabama justice and law!'.
Indianapolis Freeman column on 'the awfulness of the peonage system', citing the case among 'the worst'.
